stories.title: 🌊 Jonah 1
summaryBullets: Now the word of the Lord came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, (1:1).
“Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me.” (1:2).

But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the Lord. (1:3).
But the Lord hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up. (1:4).

Then the mariners were afraid, and each cried out to his god. And they hurled the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten it for them. But Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep. (1:5).
So the captain came and said to him, “What do you mean, you sleeper? Arise, call out to your god! Perhaps the god will give a thought to us, that we may not perish.” (1:6).
And they said to one another, “Come, let us cast lots, that we may know on whose account this evil has come upon us.” So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah. (1:7).
Then they said to him, “Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your occupation? And where do you come from? What is your country? And of what people are you?” (1:8).
And he said to them, “I am a Hebrew, and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.” (1:9).
Then the men were exceedingly afraid and said to him, “What is this that you have done!” For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them. (1:10).
Then they said to him, “What shall we do to you, that the sea may quiet down for us?” For the sea grew more and more tempestuous. (1:11).
He said to them, “Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you, for I know it is because of me that this great tempest has come upon you.” (1:12).
Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea grew more and more tempestuous against them. (1:13).
Therefore they called out to the Lord, “O Lord, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not on us innocent blood, for you, O Lord, have done as it pleased you.” (1:14).
So they picked up Jonah and hurled him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging. (1:15).
Then the men feared the Lord exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows. (1:16).
And the Lord appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights. (1:17).
crossRefs: 2 Kings 14:25 — Jonah son of Amittai mentioned in the reign of Jeroboam II.
Psalm 107:23–30 — Sailors in a storm cry out and are delivered.
Matthew 12:40 — “Sign of Jonah” (three days and three nights).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: תַּרְשִׁישׁ (Tarshish) — Greek (LXX): Θαρσείς — Aramaic: תרשיש
translationNotes.note: Distant seaport; exact location debated in antiquity. Emphasizes Jonah’s attempt to go far from his assignment.

translationNotes.term: From the presence of the LORD
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מִלִּפְנֵי יְהוָה (milifnê YHWH) — Greek (LXX): ἀπὸ προσώπου Κυρίου — Aramaic: מן קדם יי
translationNotes.note: Means fleeing the LORD’s commission/face, not denying God’s omnipresence.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: הִפִּילוּ גּוֹרָלוֹת (hippîlū gōrālōt) — Greek (LXX): ἔβαλον κλήρους — Aramaic: פלו פוריא
translationNotes.note: Ancient method to identify responsibility or make decisions (1:7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: דָּג גָּדוֹל (dag gadol) — Greek (LXX): κῆτος (kētos, ‘sea creature’) — Aramaic: נונא רבא
translationNotes.note: Not specified as a whale; a large sea creature appointed by God (1:17).

stories.keyTakeaway: Jonah flees his mission; God sends a storm; the sailors end up worshiping the LORD; a great fish swallows Jonah for three days and nights.

stories.title: 🐟 Jonah 2
summaryBullets: Then Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the belly of the fish, (2:1).
saying, (2:2).
For you cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the flood surrounded me;all your breakers and your waves passed over me. (2:3).
Then I said, ‘I am driven away from your sight;yet I shall again look upon your holy temple.’ (2:4).
The waters closed in over me to take my life; the deep surrounded me;weeds were wrapped about my head. (2:5).
To the roots of the mountains I went down, to the land whose bars closed upon me forever.Yet you brought up my life from the pit, O Lord my God. (2:6).
When my life was fainting away, I remembered the Lord,and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple. (2:7).
Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love. (2:8).
But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you;what I have vowed I will pay. Salvation belongs to the Lord!” (2:9).
And the Lord spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land. (2:10).
crossRefs: Psalm 18:4–6 — Cords of Sheol and distress in deep waters.
Psalm 42:7 — “All your waves and breakers have gone over me.”
Luke 11:30 — Jonah as a sign to a city.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שְׁאוֹל (Sheol), בּוֹר (bor, ‘pit’) — Greek (LXX): ᾅδης, λάκκος — Aramaic: שאולא, בורא
translationNotes.note: Realm of the dead / place of descent in Jonah’s prayer (2:2-6).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֶסֶד (ḥesed) — Greek (LXX): ἔλεος — Aramaic: חסדא
translationNotes.note: Covenant loyalty Jonah says idol-clingers abandon (2:8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: וַיְצַו (waytsav) — Greek (LXX): ἐνετείλατο — Aramaic: פקד
translationNotes.note: God’s direct control over the creature (2:10).

stories.keyTakeaway: Jonah prays from the depths and is delivered; the fish releases him onto land by God’s command.

stories.title: 🏙️ Jonah 3
summaryBullets: Then the word of the Lord came to Jonah the second time, saying, (3:1).
“Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it the message that I tell you.” (3:2).
So Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, according to the word of the Lord. Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city, three days' journey in breadth. (3:3).
Jonah began to go into the city, going a day's journey. And he called out, “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!” (3:4).
And the people of Nineveh believed God. They called for a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least of them. (3:5).
The word reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, removed his robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes. (3:6).

And he issued a proclamation and published through Nineveh, “By the decree of the king and his nobles: Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste anything. Let them not feed or drink water, (3:7).
but let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and let them call out mightily to God. Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands. (3:8).
Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish.” (3:9).
When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it. (3:10).
crossRefs: Jeremiah 18:7–8 — God relents concerning disaster when a nation turns from evil.
Matthew 12:41 — People of Nineveh will rise in judgment (later statement).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נֶהְפָּכֶת (nehpākhet, from הָפַךְ haphakh) — Greek (LXX): καταστραφήσεται — Aramaic: תתהפך
translationNotes.note: Can mean overturned/destroyed; the verb has a range including ‘turn/transform,’ but here announces coming ruin in forty days (3:4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: נִחָם (niḥam, ‘be moved to pity/relent’) — Greek (LXX): μετενόησεν — Aramaic: אתנחם
translationNotes.note: Human-facing language for God holding back announced disaster when people turn from evil (3:10).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חָמָס (ḥāmās) — Greek (LXX): ἀδικία/βία — Aramaic: חמסא
translationNotes.note: Named explicitly in the king’s decree as sin that must stop (3:8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַהֲלַךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים (mahalakh sheloshet yamim) — Greek (LXX): πορεία τριῶν ἡμερῶν — Aramaic: הילוך תלתא יומין
translationNotes.note: Idiomatic measure of civic size/route; indicates a very large urban area (3:3).

stories.keyTakeaway: God gives Jonah a second chance; Nineveh responds with citywide fasting and turning from evil; God relents from the announced disaster.

stories.title: 🌞 Jonah 4
summaryBullets: But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry. (4:1).

And he prayed to the Lord and said, “O Lord, is not this what I said when I was yet in my country? That is why I made haste to flee to Tarshish; for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster. (4:2).
Therefore now, O Lord, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.” (4:3).
And the Lord said, “Do you do well to be angry?” (4:4).
Jonah went out of the city and sat to the east of the city and made a booth for himself there. He sat under it in the shade, till he should see what would become of the city. (4:5).
Now the Lord God appointed a plant and made it come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head, to save him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the plant. (4:6).
But when dawn came up the next day, God appointed a worm that attacked the plant, so that it withered. (4:7).

When the sun rose, God appointed a scorching east wind, and the sun beat down on the head of Jonah so that he was faint. And he asked that he might die and said, “It is better for me to die than to live.” (4:8).
But God said to Jonah, “Do you do well to be angry for the plant?” And he said, “Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die.” (4:9).
And the Lord said, “You pity the plant, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow, which came into being in a night and perished in a night. (4:10).
And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?” (4:11).
crossRefs: Exodus 34:6–7 — God’s character formula (gracious and compassionate).
Joel 2:13 — Similar description of the LORD’s mercy.
Psalm 145:8–9 — The LORD is gracious, compassionate, and good to all.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מָנָה (manāh, ‘appoint/assign’) — Greek (LXX): κατέστησεν/διέταξεν — Aramaic: מנא
translationNotes.note: Used repeatedly: God appoints the fish, plant, worm, and east wind (1:17) (4:6–8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קִיקָיוֹן (qiqāyōn) — Greek (LXX): κολοκύνθη (var.) — Aramaic: קיקיון
translationNotes.note: Exact species uncertain (suggestions include castor-oil plant).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: קָדִים (qadīm) — Greek (LXX): καύσων/νότος (var.) — Aramaic: קדים
translationNotes.note: Hot, desiccating wind known for causing severe heat (4:8).

translationNotes.term: Do not know right hand from left
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לֹא יָדְעוּ בֵּין יְמִין לִשְׂמֹאול (lo yādaʿū bein yemin lismoʾl) — Greek (LXX): οὐκ ἴσασι δεξιὰν ἀπὸ ἀριστερᾶς — Aramaic: לא ידעין בין ימינא לשמאלא
translationNotes.note: Expression for moral/spiritual ignorance, including many children; the verse also notes many animals (4:11).

stories.keyTakeaway: God confronts Jonah’s anger with a plant, a worm, and a hot wind, ending with a question that contrasts Jonah’s short-lived pity with God’s care for a great city.
